title: The Lamp Had Not Gone Out
subtitle: 1–2 Samuel in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin: The books of Samuel begin with a woman weeping at a festival table and a boy lying down near a lamp that had not yet gone out. Then come a king hiding among the baggage, a shepherd called in from the field, five smooth stones from a brook, two friends and an arrow shot past the mark, a lame man given a place at the king's table, a prophet's story about one little ewe lamb, and a father weeping in the room over a gate. This book walks through it in forty short poems, in five parts: twenty-four from 1 Samuel and sixteen from 2 Samuel. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture.

parts.title: My Heart Exults
parts.lightHint: Beside the clay lamp that had not yet gone out in the quiet Shiloh sanctuary

parts.title: A King Like All the Nations
parts.epigraph: Make us a king to judge us like all the nations.
parts.lightName: Light of the Stone of Help
parts.lightHint: Near the upright Ebenezer witness stone in the hill pasture

parts.title: A Man After His Own Heart
parts.epigraph: Yahweh has sought for himself a man after his own heart.
parts.lightHint: Where five smooth river stones glisten in the clear valley stream

parts.title: Shepherd of My People
parts.epigraph: I took you from the sheep pen, from following the sheep, to be prince over my people.
parts.lightHint: Beside the place kept continually for Jonathan’s lame son

parts.title: My Son, My Son
parts.epigraph: Yahweh is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer.
parts.lightName: Light of the Threshing Floor Altar
parts.lightHint: Near Araunah’s threshing floor on the hill before the Finale Plaza

paintings.title: ten sons
paintings.epigraph: “Hannah, why do you weep? Why don’t you eat? Why is your heart grieved?”
paintings.poem:
every year the same road
up to Shiloh.

every year the same table,
the double portion
set in front of her,
and the same voice across the room
reminding her what she didn't have.

so she didn't eat.

her husband loved her.
am I not better to you
than ten sons? he asked.

he meant it kindly.

but some aches
aren't answered at the table.

they have to be carried
up the hill
to God.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The world measures life by speed and noise, yet 1 Samuel 1:3–8 points us to the table set before you and whispers, “they have to be carried up the hill to God.” How can you practice that unhurried wisdom today?

paintings.title: only her lips moved
paintings.epigraph: “I poured out my soul before Yahweh.”
paintings.poem:
no words came out.
only her lips moved.

the old priest watching
thought she was drunk.

she wasn't.
she was pouring.

the whole jar of it:
the years, the rival,
the empty arms,
the promise she was ready to make.

and when she stood up
she went and ate,
and her face
wasn't sad anymore.

nothing had changed yet.

except where
she had put it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The poem closes with a quiet turn: “except where she had put it.” Where in your life right now does that line hit closest to home?

paintings.title: asked of the Lord
paintings.epigraph: “I prayed for this child, and Yahweh has given me my petition which I asked of him.”
paintings.poem:
she named him Samuel:
I asked him of the Lord.

she nursed him.
she weaned him.

then she carried him up the hill
with flour and wine
and brought him to the old priest
at the same door
where she had prayed.

what she asked for,
she gave back.

not because God took it.

because she knew
whose it was
before it was ever hers.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “because she knew whose it was before it was ever hers” (1 Samuel 1:20–28) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: no rock like our God
paintings.epigraph: “He raises up the poor out of the dust.”
paintings.poem:
she didn't sing about herself.

she sang about bows
breaking in strong hands,
the full going out to work for bread,
the hungry sitting down to eat.

she sang about a God
who stoops to the dust
and lifts the poor out of it
and gives them a seat
with princes.

the barren one was singing.

she knew
which way
his hands move.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “no rock like our God” (1 Samuel 2:1–8): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “she knew which way his hands move”?

paintings.title: a little robe
paintings.epigraph: “his mother made him a little robe, and brought it to him from year to year”
paintings.poem:
every year
a little bigger.

she measured him in her mind
all year long,
guessing how much he'd grown.

then up the road to Shiloh
with the robe folded in her arms.

she gave him away
and never stopped
making him things.

that's what giving to God
looks like sometimes:

open hands,
and a needle
still moving.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Scripture remembers this moment in 1 Samuel 2:18–21 not to impress us, but to steady us: when have you seen the truth that “that's what giving to God looks like sometimes: open hands, and a needle still moving” in your own story?

paintings.title: speak
paintings.epigraph: “Speak; for your servant hears.”
paintings.poem:
the word of the Lord was rare
in those days.

the lamp hadn't gone out yet,
and a boy lay down
near the ark.

three times a voice called his name.
three times he ran
to the wrong room.

that's all right.
most of us do.

then he learned the sentence:
speak,
for your servant hears.

God wasn't waiting
for him to be older.

only to be listening.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “speak” (1 Samuel 3:1–10), what one honest sentence would you pray beside the small oil lamp in the dark after reading, “God wasn't waiting for him to be older. only to be listening”?

paintings.title: the straight way
paintings.epigraph: “The cows took the straight way by the way to Beth Shemesh.”
paintings.poem:
the ark had been taken,
and no one who took it
could keep it.

so they sent it home
on a new cart
behind two cows
that had never worn a yoke.

the cows went lowing
all the way
and didn't turn
to the right or the left.

down in the valley
the reapers looked up
from the wheat

and saw what they thought
they had lost for good

coming up the road.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Between the opening line (“the ark had been taken, and no one who took it could keep it”) and the closing thought (“down in the valley the reapers looked up from the wheat and saw what they thought they had lost for good coming up the road”), what is 1 Samuel 6:7–13 gently reframing in your own day?

paintings.title: stone of help
paintings.epigraph: “Yahweh helped us until now.”
paintings.poem:
Samuel set a stone
in a field
and gave it a name:
stone of help.

not every stone
is meant for a wall.

some are there
to be looked at,

so that on the day
you're afraid again
you can walk out to the field
and put your hand on it
and remember.

he helped us
this far.

he doesn't plan
to stop
here.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Along the road of The Lamp Had Not Gone Out, “stone of help” (1 Samuel 7:3–12) slows us down at the stones of the wall to remind us: “he doesn't plan to stop here.” Where are you being invited to trade control for trust today?

paintings.title: like everyone else
paintings.epigraph: “they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me as the king over them.”
paintings.poem:
Samuel was old.
his sons took bribes.

give us a king, the elders said,
like all the nations.

it hurt him.
he took it to God.

and God said,
it isn't you they're refusing.
it's me.

then, strangely:
listen to them.

he lets us choose.
he tells us plainly
what it will cost.

and he doesn't leave
when we choose wrong.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “like everyone else” (1 Samuel 8:4–9), what would you talk about after reading, “and he doesn't leave when we choose wrong”?

paintings.title: the lost donkeys
paintings.epigraph: “don’t set your mind on them; for they have been found.”
paintings.poem:
Saul went out
looking for donkeys.

three days of hills.
bread gone from the sacks.
nothing to show.

he was ready to turn back.

and in the town
an old seer was already waiting,
with a seat kept at the table
and a portion set aside.

your donkeys are found, he said.
don't set your mind on them.

you went out
looking for something small,

and someone
had been looking
for you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the table set before you: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “the lost donkeys”—“you went out looking for something small, and someone had been looking for you”?

paintings.title: among the baggage
paintings.epigraph: “Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage.”
paintings.poem:
the lot fell on his tribe,
then his family,
then his name.

and they couldn't find him.

the tallest man in Israel
was hiding
among the bags.

I understand him.

it's one thing
to be chosen.

it's another
to stand up
in front of everyone
and let it be true.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look at the stillness of the name by which He calls you in Timothy’s painting: what striving can you lay down as you ponder, “it's another to stand up in front of everyone and let it be true” (1 Samuel 10:20–24)?

paintings.title: seven days
paintings.epigraph: “I forced myself therefore, and offered the burnt offering.”
paintings.poem:
he waited seven days.

the enemy gathered.
the people slipped away,
a few more every morning.

and the prophet didn't come.

so he did it himself.
just this once.
he had good reasons.

the smoke was still rising
when Samuel arrived.

waiting is hardest
at the very end,

right before
the one you're waiting for
comes over the hill.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In 1 Samuel 13:8–14, the story turns on the quiet centerpiece of “seven days”—and ends with, “waiting is hardest at the very end, right before the one you're waiting for comes over the hill.” What small, unhurried faithfulness is God inviting you into today?

paintings.title: the bleating of the sheep
paintings.epigraph: “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.”
paintings.poem:
I have done
what the Lord commanded,
Saul said.

and the old man said,
then what is this bleating
in my ears?

you can bring God
the best of the flock

and still not bring him
what he asked for.

he isn't counting sheep.

he's listening
for whether
we heard him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The world measures life by speed and noise, yet 1 Samuel 15:13–22 points us to the quiet centerpiece of “the bleating of the sheep” and whispers, “he's listening for whether we heard him.” How can you practice that unhurried wisdom today?

paintings.title: Samuel mourned
paintings.epigraph: “Samuel mourned for Saul”
paintings.poem:
as Samuel turned to go,
Saul caught the edge of his robe,
and it tore.

the kingdom is torn from you
like this, Samuel said.

then he went home to Ramah
and never went to see Saul again.

but he mourned for him.

and the Lord
was grieved too.

a verdict
can be true
and still be wept over.

this one was.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The poem closes with a quiet turn: “a verdict can be true and still be wept over. this one was.” Where in your life right now does that line hit closest to home?

paintings.title: the youngest
paintings.epigraph: “man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”
paintings.poem:
seven sons walked past the prophet.

the tall one.
the strong one.
the one who looked like a king.

not this one.
not this one either.

are these all?

well, there's the youngest.
he's out with the sheep.

nobody had thought
to call him in.

so the whole feast stood waiting
until a boy came in from the field,

and God said,
this is he.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “so the whole feast stood waiting until a boy came in from the field, and God said, this is he” (1 Samuel 16:6–13) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: the harp
paintings.epigraph: “David took the harp, and played with his hand; so Saul was refreshed”
paintings.poem:
a king who couldn't rest.
a shepherd boy
with a harp.

no sermon.
no argument.
just his hand on the strings,

and the dark
lifting
for a while.

don't underestimate
what a song can do
in a troubled room.

sometimes the kindest thing
you can bring
is music,
and the patience
to keep playing.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “the harp” (1 Samuel 16:14–23): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “sometimes the kindest thing you can bring is music, and the patience to keep playing”?

paintings.title: untested
paintings.epigraph: “I can’t go with these; for I have not tested them.”
paintings.poem:
the king dressed him
in his own armor.

bronze helmet.
coat of mail.
a sword at his side.

he tried to walk
and stopped.

I can't go in these.

he took them off
and went down to the brook
with his staff in his hand.

you can't fight
in someone else's faith.

use what God
has already taught
your hands.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Scripture remembers this moment in 1 Samuel 17:38–40 not to impress us, but to steady us: when have you seen the truth that “use what God has already taught your hands” in your own story?

paintings.title: five smooth stones
paintings.epigraph: “chose for himself five smooth stones out of the brook”
paintings.poem:
he bent down at the brook
and chose five.

smooth ones.
stones the water
had been shaping
for years,

like the boy
choosing them.

across the valley
stood a man in bronze
with a spear like a weaver's beam.

you come to me with a sword, David said.
I come to you
in the name of the Lord.

the battle is his.

one stone
was enough.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “five smooth stones” (1 Samuel 17:40–50), what one honest sentence would you pray beside the quiet brook after reading, “the battle is his. one stone was enough”?

paintings.title: knit
paintings.epigraph: “the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David”
paintings.poem:
the king's son
took off his robe
and put it on the shepherd.

then his sword.
his bow.
his sash.

everything that said
this will be mine someday,
given away.

Jonathan could have seen
a rival.

he saw a friend,
and loved him
as his own soul.

there are people like this.

if you have one,
you are rich.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Between the opening line (“the king's son took off his robe and put it on the shepherd”) and the closing thought (“if you have one, you are rich”), what is 1 Samuel 18:1–4 gently reframing in your own day?

paintings.title: the arrow
paintings.epigraph: “Isn’t the arrow beyond you?”
paintings.poem:
they had agreed on a sign.
if the arrow falls short, come home.
if it flies past, go.

the arrow flew past.

a boy gathered it up
and knew nothing.

but out in the field
two friends held each other
and wept,
David the most.

go in peace, Jonathan said.
the Lord is between you and me
forever.

some goodbyes
are not an ending.

they are a promise
with a long road in it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Along the road of The Lamp Had Not Gone Out, “the arrow” (1 Samuel 20:35–42) slows us down at the quiet centerpiece of “the arrow” to remind us: “they are a promise with a long road in it.” Where are you being invited to trade control for trust today?

paintings.title: the edge of his robe
paintings.epigraph: “I will not stretch out my hand against my lord; for he is Yahweh’s anointed.”
paintings.poem:
the man hunting him
walked into the cave
where he was hiding.

this is your day,
his men whispered.

he crept close
and cut a corner
from the king's robe.

that was all.
even that troubled his heart.

outside, he held up the scrap:
see? I could have.
I didn't.

mercy isn't weakness.

it's strength
that has decided
to keep its hands open.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “the edge of his robe” (1 Samuel 24:1–12), what would you talk about after reading, “it's strength that has decided to keep its hands open”?

paintings.title: bread on the road
paintings.epigraph: “Blessed is your discretion, and blessed are you, who have kept me today from blood guiltiness”
paintings.poem:
her husband had insulted David's men,
and four hundred of them
were coming with swords.

she didn't argue.
she didn't wait.

she loaded the donkeys
with bread and raisins
and cakes of figs
and rode out to meet them.

on me be the blame, she said,
and talked an angry man
back from the edge.

some peacemakers
come with speeches.

some come with bread,
at the right hour,
on the right road.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the daily loaf broken in the hand: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “bread on the road”—“some come with bread, at the right hour, on the right road”?

paintings.title: strength in God
paintings.epigraph: “David strengthened himself in Yahweh his God.”
paintings.poem:
they came home
to smoke.

the town burned.
wives and children taken.
they wept
until they had no strength to weep.

then his own men
talked of stoning him.

no one was left
to comfort David,
so he went
to the one who was.

he didn't feel strong first.
he went to God
and found strength there.

then he asked, shall I go?
and went,
and brought them all back.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look at the stillness of the quiet centerpiece of “strength in God” in Timothy’s painting: what striving can you lay down as you ponder, “and went, and brought them all back” (1 Samuel 30:1–8)?

paintings.title: under the tamarisk
paintings.epigraph: “They took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and fasted seven days.”
paintings.poem:
Saul fell on Mount Gilboa,
and his sons with him.

long before,
when Jabesh was surrounded
and helpless,
Saul had come for them.

they remembered.

all night
the brave men of Jabesh walked,
and carried their king away,
and buried him under a tamarisk,
and fasted seven days.

whatever else
was true of Saul,

someone remembered
the day he came.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In 1 Samuel 31:1–13, the story turns on the quiet centerpiece of “under the tamarisk”—and ends with, “whatever else was true of Saul, someone remembered the day he came.” What small, unhurried faithfulness is God inviting you into today?

paintings.title: how the mighty have fallen
paintings.epigraph: “I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan.”
paintings.poem:
the man who brought the news
thought it would please him.

it didn't.

David tore his clothes
and fasted until evening,
for Saul,
who had hunted him,
and for Jonathan,
who had loved him.

then he made a song:
how the mighty have fallen.

and in the middle of it,
one line
that wasn't about kings at all:

my brother Jonathan.
you were very pleasant to me.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The world measures life by speed and noise, yet 2 Samuel 1:11–27 points us to the quiet centerpiece of “how the mighty have fallen” and whispers, “you were very pleasant to me.” How can you practice that unhurried wisdom today?

paintings.title: bone and flesh
paintings.epigraph: “You will be shepherd of my people Israel”
paintings.poem:
all the tribes came to Hebron
and said,
we are your bone and your flesh.

years of running
ended at a gate.

they didn't ask him
to be a warrior.
he was already that.

they reminded him
what God had said:
you will shepherd my people.

the crown
was a bigger field.

the work
was the same.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The poem closes with a quiet turn: “they reminded him what God had said: you will shepherd my people. the work was the same.” Where in your life right now does that line hit closest to home?

paintings.title: the sound in the treetops
paintings.epigraph: “When you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the mulberry trees, then stir yourself up”
paintings.poem:
the same enemy.
the same valley.

last time God said,
go up.

this time he said,
circle around.
wait by the trees.
when you hear marching
in the tops of the leaves,
move.

David asked again.
he didn't assume.

yesterday's answer
isn't always
today's.

so he listened
for the wind.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “so he listened for the wind” (2 Samuel 5:22–25) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: with all his might
paintings.epigraph: “David danced before Yahweh with all his might”
paintings.poem:
the ark came up the road,
and the king
couldn't keep still.

a linen ephod,
nothing grand,
leaping and dancing
in front of everyone.

from her window
Michal looked down
and despised him.

it was before the Lord, he said.
I'll be humbler still.

then he gave bread
and dates and raisins
to every person there.

joy that is real
spills over
into everyone's hands.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “with all his might” (2 Samuel 6:12–22): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “joy that is real spills over into everyone's hands”?

paintings.title: who am I
paintings.epigraph: “Who am I, Lord Yahweh, and what is my house, that you have brought me this far?”
paintings.poem:
I live in cedar, the king said,
and God lives in a tent.
let me build him a house.

that night the answer came:
I never asked for one.

I took you
from following the sheep.
I have been with you
wherever you went.

you won't build me a house.
I will build you one.

and David went in
and sat before the Lord
and could only say,

who am I,
that you have brought me
this far?
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Scripture remembers this moment in 2 Samuel 7:1–18 not to impress us, but to steady us: when have you seen the truth that “and David went in and sat before the Lord and could only say, who am I, that you have brought me this far?” in your own story?

paintings.title: at the king's table
paintings.epigraph: “You will eat bread at my table continually.”
paintings.poem:
is there anyone left
of Saul's house,
that I may show him kindness
for Jonathan's sake?

there was.
a son,
lame in both feet,
living far away in Lo Debar.

he bowed to the ground
and called himself a dead dog.

David called him by name.
don't be afraid.
you will eat at my table.

a place set every day
for a promise
made to a friend

long after
the friend was gone.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “at the king's table” (2 Samuel 9:1–13), what one honest sentence would you pray beside the table set before you after reading, “a place set every day for a promise made to a friend long after the friend was gone”?

paintings.title: until your beards have grown
paintings.epigraph: “Wait at Jericho until your beards have grown, and then return.”
paintings.poem:
he sent them
to comfort a grieving king.

they came back shamed,
half their beards shaved away,
their robes cut short.

David didn't make them
walk through Jerusalem
like that.

stay at Jericho, he said.
come home
when your beards have grown.

there is a kind of mercy
that asks no questions,

just gives you time,
and a place to wait,
until you feel
like yourself again.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Between the opening line (“he sent them to comfort a grieving king”) and the closing thought (“there is a kind of mercy that asks no questions, just gives you time, and a place to wait, until you feel like yourself again”), what is 2 Samuel 10:1–5 gently reframing in your own day?

paintings.title: when kings go out
paintings.epigraph: “But David stayed at Jerusalem.”
paintings.poem:
it was the season
when kings went out to war.

David stayed home.

one evening, restless,
he walked on the roof,
and saw,
and asked,
and sent.

not one great fall,
but small steps,
each one easier
than it should have been,

until a faithful soldier
carried a letter
to his own death.

the worst thing David ever did
began on a quiet evening
with nothing to do.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Along the road of The Lamp Had Not Gone Out, “when kings go out” (2 Samuel 11:1–17) slows us down at the quiet centerpiece of “when kings go out” to remind us: “the worst thing David ever did began on a quiet evening with nothing to do.” Where are you being invited to trade control for trust today?

paintings.title: you are the man
paintings.epigraph: “You are the man.”
paintings.poem:
Nathan told a story.

a poor man.
one little ewe lamb.
it ate his food
and drank from his cup
and slept in his arms
like a daughter.

and a rich man
with flocks and herds
who took it anyway.

that man deserves to die! the king said.

and the prophet said,
you are the man.

no more hiding then.
I have sinned against the Lord.

and the answer came just as quickly:
the Lord has put away your sin.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “you are the man” (2 Samuel 12:1–13), what would you talk about after reading, “and the answer came just as quickly: the Lord has put away your sin”?

paintings.title: I will go to him
paintings.epigraph: “I will go to him, but he will not return to me.”
paintings.poem:
seven days on the ground, fasting.

then whispering in the hall,
and he knew.

he got up.
he washed.
he changed his clothes,
went to worship,
and ate.

while he was alive, I hoped, he said.
now,
can I bring him back?

I will go to him.
he will not come to me.

the grief didn't end there.

but now
it had somewhere
to go.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the quiet centerpiece of “I will go to him”: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “I will go to him”—“but now it had somewhere to go”?

paintings.title: here I am
paintings.epigraph: “behold, here I am. Let him do to me as seems good to him.”
paintings.poem:
his own son
had stolen the hearts of Israel.

the priests came out
carrying the ark,
and David sent it back.

if God is pleased with me,
he'll bring me home to see it.
if not,
here I am.

then he climbed the Mount of Olives
barefoot,
weeping as he went.

he didn't carry God along
like a charm.

he put himself
in God's hands
and walked.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look at the stillness of the gnarled olive tree in Timothy’s painting: what striving can you lay down as you ponder, “he put himself in God's hands and walked” (2 Samuel 15:23–30)?

paintings.title: deal gently
paintings.epigraph: “Deal gently for my sake with the young man, even with Absalom.”
paintings.poem:
the son had come against the father
with an army.

and the father
stood by the gate
as his men marched out
and said to every captain,
where all could hear:

deal gently
with the young man.
for my sake.

not the rebel.
not the enemy.
the young man.

he was fighting
for his life,

and still trying to save
the one
who had come to take it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In 2 Samuel 18:1–5, the story turns on the city gate—and ends with, “he was fighting for his life, and still trying to save the one who had come to take it.” What small, unhurried faithfulness is God inviting you into today?

paintings.title: my son, my son
paintings.epigraph: “My son, my son Absalom!”
paintings.poem:
two runners came.

the king asked each one
the same question:
is it well with the young man?

and when he understood,
he climbed to the room over the gate
and wept.

my son, my son.
I wish I had died
instead of you.

the battle was won.
it didn't reach that room.

no one grieves like that
for an enemy.

only for a child
they never stopped
waiting for.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The world measures life by speed and noise, yet 2 Samuel 18:24–33 points us to the stone well in the heat of the day and whispers, “only for a child they never stopped waiting for.” How can you practice that unhurried wisdom today?

paintings.title: my lamp
paintings.epigraph: “For you are my lamp, Yahweh. Yahweh will light up my darkness.”
paintings.poem:
long ago in Shiloh
a boy named Samuel
slept near a lamp
that hadn't gone out yet.

now David,
looking back
over caves and wars
and his own worst days,

sings:

you are my lamp, Lord.
you light up my darkness.

not, you took the darkness away.

you lit it.

and that was enough
to walk by.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The poem closes with a quiet turn: “and that was enough to walk by.” Where in your life right now does that line hit closest to home?

paintings.title: water from Bethlehem
paintings.epigraph: “he would not drink of it, but poured it out to Yahweh.”
paintings.poem:
hiding in a cave,
he said it almost to himself:
if only someone would bring me water
from the well by the gate
in Bethlehem.

three of his men heard.
they broke through the enemy camp
and brought it back.

and he couldn't drink it.

he poured it out
on the ground
before the Lord.

these men risked their lives.
it isn't mine to drink.

some gifts are too holy to keep.

you give them
back to God.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “you give them back to God” (2 Samuel 23:13–17) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: nothing
paintings.epigraph: “I will not offer burnt offerings to Yahweh my God which cost me nothing.”
paintings.poem:
the plague stopped
at a farmer's threshing floor.

take it, the farmer said.
the oxen too.
the yokes for wood.
all of it, free.

no, said the king.
I'll pay.

I will not give the Lord
what cost me nothing.

he counted out the silver
and built his altar there,
on the hill
where one day
his son would build
a house for God.

and the plague was lifted
from the land.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “nothing” (2 Samuel 24:18–25): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “and the plague was lifted from the land”?
